definition.text: Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants, through evaporation and transpiration.

facts.text: Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies, while transpiration moves water from roots through a plant and out of its stomata as vapour.
Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of rain and snow falling on land returns to the air this way.
It is measured in millimetres of water over a set time.
Its level depends mainly on how much water is available, how much energy is in the air and soil, and how much moisture the air can take up.
Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the effects of climate change on the water cycle.
Measuring it is key to water resource management and irrigation planning.

title: Vegetation and evapotranspiration

definition.text: The type and density of vegetation strongly shape evapotranspiration and so how much water a landscape yields.

facts.text: Dense vegetation such as forest may raise evapotranspiration and reduce water yield.
Rainforests are an exception: they raise humidity, cool the ground and slow winds, increasing stream flows and groundwater while they stand.
Clearing rainforests often leads to desertification as soils dry out and erode.
Deforestation lowers evapotranspiration and so atmospheric moisture, which can reduce rain downwind.

related: Land use effects on the water cycle

definition.text: Potential evapotranspiration is the amount of water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if enough water were available.

facts.text: It measures the air's demand for moisture, while actual evapotranspiration also depends on how much water the surface can supply.
Actual evapotranspiration can never exceed the potential, but can fall below it when water is short.
A dryland is a place where yearly potential evaporation exceeds yearly precipitation.
It is higher in summer, on clear and windy days, and nearer the equator.

definition.text: Because water vapour flow is hard to measure directly, evapotranspiration is usually estimated indirectly.

facts.text: A catchment water balance relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and groundwater recharge, so ET can be solved for.
Energy balance methods, including the satellite-based SEBAL and METRIC algorithms, map ET pixel by pixel.
The Penman–Monteith equation, recommended by the FAO, calculates reference ET from weather data.
Weighing lysimeters measure it directly but only over small areas.

title: Haber process

definition.text: The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, is the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen.

facts.text: It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, and most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer.
Fritz Haber showed it working in the laboratory in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF.
It met rising demand for fertilizer when mined niter and guano were thought too scarce for future needs.
The hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012.
Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas.
As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
distinct_from: Economic and environmental effects of the Haber process

title: Economic and environmental effects of the Haber process

definition.text: Synthetic fertilizer from the Haber process greatly raised farm productivity and population, at the cost of energy use and nitrogen pollution.

facts.text: Vaclav Smil estimated that at 1900 yields, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land.
Called the detonator of the population explosion, it helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018.
Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues came from the process.
Without it, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people.
It is one of the largest sources of reactive nitrogen build-up; because crops use less than 50% of applied nitrogen, runoff harms habitats.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer causes around 5% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
Cheap synthetic fertilizer weakens farmers' incentive to rotate in nitrogen-fixing legumes.
Haber-process fertilizer is a typical high-carbon import that a carbon tariff might cover.
